new_statements.rule_in_words: In words elicited in isolation, stress falls on the final syllable of the word in the Lebu' Vu' (Long Sela'an / Long Ikang) and Long San dialects; the author records no exceptions. Whether this final stress persists in connected speech is not addressed in the article (Blust 2013 suggests penultimate stress in phrasal context for languages of this type).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated ('invariably'). The underlying notebook (RB2-003-C, downloaded) shows a handful of penultimate stress ticks ('ŋan 'sky?', 'uʔban, Long Ikang 'piʔən 'nine') among overwhelmingly final ticks.
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms only (elicited wordlist forms from Blust's 1971 fieldwork at Long Sela'an, Long Ikang and Long San). Blust 2013 (sec. 4, Borneo) states as an areal generalisation that such Sarawak languages have final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context, and that stress is not phonemic in any language of Borneo; Blust 2017 itself gives no phrasal data. The conflicting report 'regular penultimate stress but shifts to the final syllable if the penult is an open schwa syllable' (Smith 2020 AFLA 27 handout p.12; Kroeger & Smith 2024 snippet, both from Blust n.d.) is about Long Wat, a different Lowland Kenyah variety (Blust's Type B, closer to Sebop) that only shares the ISO code.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog long1406 'Western Lowland Kenyah' is scoped to Lebo' Vo' (Lebu' Vu', 'Long San Kenyah'): the Long San, Long Selaan and Long Ikang communities on the upper Baram (Smith 2017 p.14; Glottolog alt names; Blust 2017 'Lebu' Vu' Kenyah at Long Sela'an and Long Ikang, and the Long Tikan Kenyah at Long San'). The quoted statement (Blust 2017 fn. 11) is about exactly these three villages (Blust's Lowland Kenyah Type A). The ISO 639-3 code [ttw] was, however, defined on 'Long Wat' (CR 2007-247: one community on the Apoh, a Tutoh tributary, 'more closely related to Sebop and Penan'); Long Wat is Blust's Lowland Type B (Long Sela'an-Long Wat cognacy 61%, Long Wat-Sebop 75% in Blust 1974 via Kroeger 1998) and Smith 2015/2017 list it with Penan-Sebop, while Glottolog keeps 'Long Wat' only as a lexvo alternative name of long1406 and gives Sebop its own code sebo1238. The Long Wat stress rule (penultimate, shifting to final after an open schwa penult: Smith 2020 handout p.12; Kroeger & Smith 2024 snippet, both from Blust n.d.) therefore describes a variety that shares the ISO code but not the Glottolog referent, and it conflicts with the Lebo' Vo' report.

new_statements.relation_note: Variety caveat: this section is Long Wat (Apoh, Tutoh), the ISO [ttw] reference variety and a Glottolog alt name of long1406, but Blust's Lowland Type B, which Smith 2015/2017 place with Sebop-Penan rather than with Lebo' Vo'; Blust 2017 fn. 7 leaves open whether it is the same language as Long Sela'an. No prose rule, so the notebook refines rather than settles: it documents both patterns for Long Wat and confirms that Blust's 1971 citat…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The notebook gives no rule, only stress ticks on citation forms. Two patterns coexist: in the first session (pp. 11-12) stress is penultimate ('luəh, 'tujək, 'ayəh, 'piʔən, 'bulun, 'batəw, 'basaʔ, 'laŋit, 'likud, 'anak) and shifts to the final syllable only when the penult vowel is schwa (tə'ləw, lə'məh, jə'ñãp, tə'bəw, kə'lunan, jə'lo), which is exactly the rule Smith 2020 attributes to Long Wat; but from the lexicostatistical list onward (pp. 13-22) the ticks are predominantly FINAL whatever the penult vowel (ku'lit, bu'ré, tu'lay, a'tay, mu'rip, mi'ré, ma'pip, bu'lun, bu'řuk, la'ʔun, ka'yəw, la'kat, tu'lin, ba'təw, ba'way, su'ŋay, ma'ʔay, ba'səʔ, pa'dəy, pu'téʔ, ka'pan, ja'ʔət, u'man, la'yuk, sa'ʔay, roughly 90 items) with a minority of penult ticks ('satuəy, 'musoʔ, 'pusoʔ, 'jipən, 'kuman, 'iŋən, 'tinən, 'tamən, 'matay, 'sagãʔ, 'juit, 'ñipah, 'kutəw, 'biuʔ). The same lexeme is ticked both ways: 'bulun p. 11 vs bu'lun p. 16, 'batəw p. 11 vs ba'təw p. 17, 'basaʔ p. 12 vs ba'səʔ p. 18. Taken as a whole the citation-form ticks lean final, in line with Blust 2017 fn. 11 for Long Sela'an and Blust 2013's areal remark on final citation-form stress in Sarawak, but the data are not consistent enough to read a single rule off them.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none marked; one double tick ''jato '100' p. 11 and one 'la'kéy 'man' p. 12 (flagged '?' by Blust), otherwise no secondary-stress notation
new_statements.exceptions: Blust marks no exceptions in prose. Observed: schwa-penult forms are always ticked final (tə'ləw, lə'məh, tə'bəw, kə'lunan, jə'lo, sə'git, mə'day, pə'sak, mə'səp, mə'san, pə'gən, mə'daʔ, mə'kut, mə'nat); some forms carry both readings across sessions (bulun, batəw, basaʔ); ticks stop entirely after p. 22, and the p. 68 note on stressed long vowels concerns Long Napir (LN) and Bintulu (BK), not Kenyah.
new_statements.identity_note: Work 0 describes Lebo' Vo' Kenyah of Long San (readme; consultant Louise Ping Laing), i.e. long1406 proper, although the ScholarSpace metadata tags it 'Mainstream Kenyah' [xkl]. Work 1 describes Long Wat (Apoh branch of the Tutoh, speaker Win Karang, 1971): the ISO [ttw] reference variety and a Glottolog long1406 alt name, but Blust's Lowland Type B, grouped with Sebop-Penan by Smith 2015/2017 and of uncertain language status relative to Long Sela'an per Blust 2017 fn. 7. The p. 68 stress note in the notebook is about Long Napir and Bintulu, not Kenyah.

readall_conflicts: The two newly opened works do not state a rule. Laing 2022 is silent. Blust's 1971 Long Wat notebook (RB2-003-E) is internally mixed: the first elicitation page (p. 11-12) ticks penultimate stress with a shift to final on schwa penults, the pattern Smith 2020 (AFLA handout p. 12) reports for Long Wat from Blust's notes and that Smith 2022 generalises to Kenyah, whereas the lexicostatistical list pp. 13-22 ticks final stress on most items regardless of penult vowel, matching the catalog's fixed: final syllable record (Blust 2017 fn. 11 for Long Sela'an: 'Stress was invariably recorded as final in citation forms') and the earlier notebook C reading for Long Selaan/Long Ikang. So the live disagreement remains the one already held by the project: Blust's citation-form transcriptions (final) versus Smith's penult-with-schwa-shift rule for Long Wat; the notebook shows both patterns in the same speaker's data, and it is a Long Wat (Type B) source, not Lebo' Vo' proper.

sources.note: p.12: 'Kenyah (Long Wat dialect, Sarawak) has regular penultimate stress but shifts stress to the final syllable if the penultimate syllable is open with a schwa nucleus.' Examples *təlu > tələ́w 'three', *CəbuS > təbə́w 'sugarcane' vs *duSa > lúəh 'two', *bulu(-n) > búlun 'body hair'.
